source.title: The Optimality of (Accelerated) SGD for High-Dimensional Quadratic Optimization
source.authors: Hai-Han Zhang; Yuan-Shi Liu; Qianwen Chen; Cong Fang

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own theoretical and experimental results on SGD/SHB generalization and optimization in high-dimensional quadratic problems, including a CIFAR-2 neural-network experiment. This is an extension to a setting outside the claim versions' specified benchmarks and comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper's theoretical optimality results and its own synthetic quadratic and CIFAR-2 experiments bear on generalization or optimizer effects. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows. Figure 5.1 and Figure 6.1(d) are described in text but do not give numeric plotted values, so rows preserve the stated qualitative results.
record.test_reason: The study tests optimality of SGD and Heavy Ball momentum on quadratic problems and compares their CIFAR-2 test losses. None of V1–V8 names this comparison. In particular, V4 requires adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD; Heavy Ball momentum is not an adaptive optimizer.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but should specify that minimax optimality holds up to polylogarithmic factors under the stated assumptions and parameter choices. The authors establish optimality in specified high-dimensional quadratic regimes and report a qualitative CIFAR-2 benefit from momentum. They leave a > 2b for future work and conjecture that additional computational resources are required.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies stochastic quadratic optimization with exponentially decaying step size and Heavy Ball momentum, and includes a two-layer ReLU network experiment in an NTK regime. It does not reproduce the claim versions' experiments or methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that momentum changes the theoretical bias-variance trade-off; in the CIFAR-2 experiment it tests β = 0.5 and 0.9, but the prose does not report separate outcomes for those settings. Synthetic results also vary with noise, Hessian spectrum, source condition, momentum and initial step size.

fits_no_version.finding: Under anisotropic gradient noise and constant noise level, the theory establishes minimax optimality up to polylogarithmic factors for SGD when a ≤ b and appropriately configured SHB when b < a ≤ 2b. Synthetic experiments examine these rates and sensitivity to momentum and initial step size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For specified high-dimensional quadratic function classes, exponentially decaying step sizes and suitable momentum yield statistically optimal convergence rates in defined spectral and source-condition regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.2 reports that adding momentum improves convergence and performance in a one-epoch CIFAR-2 experiment using a width-1024 two-layer ReLU network; Figure 6.1(d) measures test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heavy Ball momentum can improve test-loss performance over SGD in the tested CIFAR-2 training setting.

record.problems: The CIFAR-2 result is presented only as a plotted test-loss comparison, without numeric values or uncertainty; the text does not separate the reported improvement by the two tested momentum settings. The synthetic experiments repeat each experiment five times and report averages, but the excerpted descriptions do not give uncertainty for individual results beyond the figure caption's one-standard-deviation shading.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible additional results from the paper's theoretical bounds or synthetic experiments were omitted: they concern quadratic excess risk and are recorded under fits_no_version because the supplied versions do not name those findings. Figure 5.1's synthetic experiment descriptions are likewise not rows for the versions tested here.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error across widths beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
All parts: no adaptive optimizer comparison, tuning-budget comparison, switching intervention, or decoupled weight-decay intervention.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness versus train-test gaps and competing measures.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized examples versus matched random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Generalization results alone do not establish a test of these specific versions. The fixed network width, batch size, and epoch budget are experimental settings, not interventions testing V2 or V5. The supplied figure caption identifies test loss, but the extracted text supplies neither plotted values nor separate outcomes for each momentum setting.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep beyond interpolation or test-error comparison across widths.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
The paper compares SGD and momentum SHB in its CIFAR-2 NTK-regime experiment, but does not test Adam or other adaptive optimizers, limited tuning, language benchmarks, or weight-decay recovery.
No batch-size sweep or large-batch comparison.
No sharpness or other measured-property comparison against train-test generalization gaps.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-2 with exponentially decaying step size; batch size 10 and epoch 1.

conditions.value: CIFAR-2; 10,000 training samples and 2,000 test samples

rows.measure: Test loss; qualitative comparison stated, numeric value not given in text.
rows.value: SGD test loss shown in Figure 6.1(d); text says adding momentum accelerates SGD and achieves better performance.
rows.note: The prose compares momentum-added SHB against SGD, but does not state the values or explicitly identify which plotted metric constitutes the reported better performance.
rows.check: SGD is an optimizer, not a model. Its test-loss curve provides a baseline for the momentum comparison, but no adaptive optimizer is tested, so this row cannot assess V4. Numerical loss values are unavailable in the supplied text.
